title: Checkpoint: Relations, Equivalence, and Invariants
learningObjective: Demonstrate mastery of relation properties, equivalence relations, and invariant arguments from this module by identifying, proving, and disproving them without further scaffolding.

retrieve.bodyMarkdown: This checkpoint draws on both lessons of this module: relation properties (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), equivalence relations and their classes, and invariant arguments for disproving equivalence.

encounter.bodyMarkdown: No new puzzle here — this checkpoint asks you to apply what you've already worked out about "$\equiv \pmod n$"-style relations to a fresh relation and a fresh pair of numbers, without the lesson's scaffolding.

explain.bodyMarkdown: No new theory. Use the definitions of reflexive/symmetric/transitive, equivalence relation, and invariant argument exactly as given in Lessons 1 and 2 of this module.

reflect.bodyMarkdown: If any of these problems felt unfamiliar, revisit the corresponding lesson before moving to the next module: relation properties and direct verification (Lesson 1), or equivalence relations and invariant arguments (Lesson 2).

problems.promptMarkdown: Which of the following relations on $\mathbb{Z}$ is an equivalence relation?

options.label: $a \sim b \iff a \leq b$
options.accessibleLabel: a is related to b iff a is less than or equal to b.

options.label: $a \sim b \iff a - b$ is even
options.accessibleLabel: a is related to b iff a minus b is even.

options.label: $a \sim b \iff a \mid b$
options.accessibleLabel: a is related to b iff a divides b.

options.label: $a \sim b \iff a \neq b$
options.accessibleLabel: a is related to b iff a does not equal b.

hints.bodyMarkdown: Check reflexivity first for each option — this alone eliminates one of them immediately.
For (a), is $2 \leq 1$ true when $1 \leq 2$ is true? For (c), does $2 \mid 4$ imply $4 \mid 2$? For (d), is $a \neq a$ ever true?
(a) fails symmetry (like $<$, $\leq$ isn't symmetric). (c) fails symmetry, as shown in Lesson 1. (d) fails reflexivity, since $a \neq a$ is always false.

(b) is reflexive ($a-a=0$ is even), symmetric ($a-b$ even $\Rightarrow$ $b-a=-(a-b)$ is even), and transitive (sum of two even numbers is even) — it's an equivalence relation, matching "same parity" from Lesson 2.

problems.solutionMarkdown: (a) $a \leq b$ is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric ($1 \leq 2$ doesn't give $2 \leq 1$). (c) $a \mid b$ is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric, as shown in Lesson 1. (d) $a \neq b$ is not even reflexive, since $a \neq a$ is always false. (b) $a - b$ even is reflexive ($a-a=0$, even), symmetric (if $a-b$ is even then $b-a=-(a-b)$ is also even), and transitive (if $a-b$ and $b-c$ are even, their sum $a-c$ is even) — it is an equivalence relation (the same-parity relation from Lesson 2).

problems.promptMarkdown: Arrange the steps of a direct proof that $a \sim b \iff a - b$ is even is transitive on $\mathbb{Z}$.

steps.textMarkdown: Assume $a - b$ is even and $b - c$ is even.
By definition, $a - b = 2k$ and $b - c = 2j$ for some integers $k, j$.
Since $k+j$ is an integer, $a-c$ is even, so $a \sim c$.

hints.bodyMarkdown: This mirrors the transitivity proof for $\equiv \pmod 5$ from Lesson 1, but with the definition of "even" instead of "divisible by 5".
Start by assuming both hypotheses, then unpack each with the definition of even, introducing witness integers.
Add the two witness equations to eliminate $b$ and produce an expression for $a-c$.
Order: assume both hypotheses, rewrite with witnesses $k,j$, add to get $a-c=2(k+j)$, then conclude $a \sim c$ by definition.

problems.solutionMarkdown: Assume $a-b$ and $b-c$ are both even, so $a-b=2k$ and $b-c=2j$ for integers $k,j$. Adding: $a-c = (a-b)+(b-c) = 2k+2j = 2(k+j)$. Since $k+j$ is an integer, $a-c$ is even, so $a \sim c$. This is exactly the same argument shape as the mod-5 transitivity proof from Lesson 1, applied to the invariant "even/odd" instead of "remainder mod 5".

problems.promptMarkdown: Use an invariant argument to show $13$ and $20$ are not related under $a \sim b \iff a - b$ is even: $13$ is ___ (even/odd) and $20$ is ___ (even/odd), and since these differ, $13 \not\sim 20$.

hints.bodyMarkdown: The invariant preserved by this relation is parity (even or odd) — two related numbers must share it.
Determine the parity of each number individually first.
$13 = 2\cdot 6 + 1$; $20 = 2 \cdot 10$. What does each remainder tell you about parity?
$13$ is odd, $20$ is even — different parities mean $13 - 20$ is odd (in fact $13-20=-7$), not even, so $13 \not\sim 20$.

problems.solutionMarkdown: $13$ is odd (it equals $2\cdot6+1$) and $20$ is even (it equals $2\cdot10$). Since these two numbers have different values of the invariant "parity," they cannot be related by $a \sim b \iff a-b$ is even — and indeed $13-20=-7$, which is odd, confirming $13 \not\sim 20$.
